clue.text: Novelist went up to historian

parts.note: went up means rose, past tense of rise
Thomas Babington Macaulay, the Victorian historian of England

explanation.surface: Some writer climbed up to meet a scholar of the past.
explanation.definitionFit: Dame Rose Macaulay was an English writer of fiction, author of The Towers of Trebizond.

clue.text: Audience for Victorian novelist at Royal Society

parts.note: Charles Reade, author of The Cloister and the Hearth
RS is the standard abbreviation for the Royal Society, Britain's scientific academy

explanation.surface: A Victorian writer gives a talk to the assembled scientists of the Royal Society.
explanation.definitionFit: Those who take in a book make up its public, the people it is written for.

clue.text: Stevenson club with dwindling membership?

parts.note: R. L. Stevenson wrote stories about a club whose members agree to be killed off, so its numbers shrink

explanation.surface: A society founded by Stevenson is losing members.
explanation.walkthrough: Robert Louis Stevenson's New Arabian Nights includes a tale of a club for people wishing to die; a membership that takes its own lives must dwindle.
explanation.definitionFit: The club in Stevenson's story exists for self-destruction, so its members are taking their own lives.

clue.text: How Marquéz wrote and realistically

parts.note: the label for García Márquez's style pairs a word for wondrous enchantment with realism, here as two adverbs

explanation.surface: A question of style: how the Colombian novelist wrote, and how true to life.
explanation.walkthrough: Gabriel García Márquez is the great name of magic realism; the clue turns the style's label into 'wrote ___ and realistically'.
explanation.definitionFit: Magic realism blends wonders with everyday life, so Márquez wrote by enchantment as well as with realism.

clue.text: What Nell Dunn's Joy never was

definitions.text: What Nell Dunn's Joy never was

parts.words: What Nell Dunn's Joy never was
parts.note: Joy is the heroine of Nell Dunn's novel Poor Cow; she is never intimidated, so the title animal becomes a past participle

explanation.surface: A remark on the indomitable heroine of a 1960s novel.
explanation.walkthrough: Nell Dunn's 1967 novel Poor Cow follows Joy, a young London mother; the clue plays on the title, since for all her troubles she is never subdued.
explanation.definitionFit: Joy stays spirited and unbowed, never frightened into submission despite her hard life.

clue.text: British geological feature immortalized by Wodehouse

parts.note: UK, the United Kingdom, stands for British
a ridge is a long raised crest of land

explanation.surface: A landmark of the English countryside made famous by P. G. Wodehouse.
explanation.definitionFit: Stanley Featherstonehaugh Ukridge is the scheming hero of a series of Wodehouse stories.

clue.text: Flying heart doctors

parts.note: winged cupids who fly about and treat the heart by making people fall in love with their arrows

explanation.surface: Airborne cardiac surgeons rushing to an emergency.
explanation.walkthrough: The cupids of Italian art work on hearts with their arrows, so they are winged physicians of love.
explanation.definitionFit: Amorini are the little winged cupids of Renaissance painting and sculpture.

clue.text: Pinnacle of existence, due to brainwork, say

definitions.meaning: the highest state of living, success at the summit of society
'brainwork' sounds like Braine work: John Braine's 1962 novel, sequel to Room at the Top

explanation.surface: Reaching the summit of one's life thanks to hard thinking.
explanation.walkthrough: John Braine wrote Room at the Top and its sequel; 'brainwork, say' asks for something by Braine.
explanation.definitionFit: Both the summit of a successful career and the title of John Braine's 1962 novel.

clue.text: Describing how I introduce little review with mixed gin

indicators.note: the I comes first in the clue and leads in what follows, introducing the little review after it

parts.note: a review is a periodical, and a little one is shortened to mag, for magazine

indicators.note: mixed tells us the three letters of gin are stirred into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone explains how they launch a small magazine over a gin cocktail.
explanation.definitionFit: Picturing or portraying something in words or images is depicting it.

clue.text: Piracy the and war gave place politics and -—too the law-lord (Emerson, English Traits)

annotationWithheld.why: Piracy the and war gave place politics and -—too the law-lord (Emerson, English Traits) (7): OCR has scrambled Emerson's sentence ('Piracy and war gave place to trade, politics and letters; the war-lord to the law-lord'), and there is no scan to restore the printed clue
annotationWithheld.clue: Piracy the and war gave place politics and -—too the law-lord (Emerson, English Traits)

clue.text: Strange, rigid lessons from radical feminist

indicators.note: strange signals that the letters of the following words are made odd, rearranged

explanation.surface: Peculiar, inflexible teachings handed down by a militant feminist.
explanation.definitionFit: The Nobel laureate author of The Golden Notebook was taken up as a feminist icon.

clue.text: Referring to a gray thought in a green shade?

definitions.text: Referring to a gray thought in a green shade?

parts.words: Referring to a gray thought in a green shade?
parts.note: Marvell's 'a green thought in a green shade' is altered to a gray one, pointing to Thomas Gray's churchyard poem of mourning

explanation.surface: A melancholy musing in a leafy garden, after Marvell.
explanation.walkthrough: Marvell's The Garden has 'a green thought in a green shade'; making it 'gray' points to Gray's Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard, so the adjective describing it is wanted.
explanation.definitionFit: Gray's poem is the great English elegy, so a 'gray thought' is mournful and lamenting.

clue.text: Even less reliable than Jack Dawkins?

definitions.text: Even less reliable than Jack Dawkins?

parts.words: Even less reliable than Jack Dawkins?
parts.note: Jack Dawkins is the Artful Dodger of Oliver Twist; one who outdoes him is more of a Dodger

explanation.surface: Someone even shiftier than Dickens's young pickpocket.
explanation.walkthrough: Jack Dawkins is the real name of the Artful Dodger in Oliver Twist; the comparative of 'Dodger' read as an adjective gives the word for less trustworthy.
explanation.definitionFit: Something shady or untrustworthy is described by the informal word, here in its comparative form.

clue.text: Characterized as ghastly good by Betjeman

definitions.text: Characterized as ghastly good by Betjeman

parts.words: Characterized as ghastly good by Betjeman
parts.note: John Betjeman's 1933 book on architecture is titled Ghastly Good ..., a word for aesthetic judgment

explanation.surface: A poet passes judgment on something both awful and fine.
explanation.walkthrough: John Betjeman's first prose book, on English architecture, was Ghastly Good ___ (1933).
explanation.definitionFit: Aesthetic discernment, the sense of what is fine or vulgar, is what Betjeman's title pairs with 'ghastly good'.

clue.text: Money gets suit back for suicidal poet

parts.note: lucre is money, as in filthy lucre

indicators.note: back says the word suit is written in reverse order

explanation.surface: Cash buys a garment for a poet in despair.
explanation.walkthrough: 'suit' poses as clothing bought with the cash; 'back' turns it round. 'suicidal' fits because St Jerome reported the Roman poet killed himself.
explanation.definitionFit: The Roman author of De Rerum Natura is said by Jerome to have taken his own life.

clue.text: Rich clone cobbled together from Holinshed, perhaps

indicators.note: cobbled together means roughly assembled, so the letters of the two words are rearranged

explanation.surface: A wealthy copy is crudely assembled from an Elizabethan source.
explanation.definitionFit: Raphael Holinshed's historical record of England, Scotland and Ireland was Shakespeare's source for many plays.

clue.text: Susan Howatch's take on Icarus?

parts.note: Susan Howatch wrote a 1999 novel of ambition, and Icarus flew too near the sun

explanation.surface: A novelist retells the myth of the boy who flew too close to the sun.
explanation.walkthrough: Susan Howatch's novel The High Flyer (1999) is about an ambitious lawyer; Icarus is the mythical figure who soared too high on wax wings.
explanation.definitionFit: An ambitious achiever soars, and Icarus literally flew higher than was safe.

clue.text: "Find — out a sunny seat, / With babe and lambkin at her feet.. coleridge"

definitions.text: Find — out a sunny seat, / With babe and lambkin at her feet.. coleridge

parts.words: Find — out a sunny seat, / With babe and lambkin at her feet.. coleridge
parts.note: the gap in Coleridge's lines is an old woman addressed by an archaic dialect word for grandmother

explanation.surface: Lines of Coleridge inviting an old woman to sit in the sun.
explanation.walkthrough: A fill-in: the missing word in Coleridge's couplet is the old word for a grandmother, used in Shakespeare's day and later.
explanation.definitionFit: An archaic term for a grandmother or old woman, fitting a figure with babe and lambkin at her feet.

clue.text: Paper size for a London apprentice

definitions.meaning: a size of writing paper, about 14 by 17 inches
Elizabethan statutes made London apprentices wear a round woollen cap

explanation.surface: Choosing what sheets of paper to give a young trainee in the capital.
explanation.definitionFit: Both an old paper size and the woollen cap worn by apprentices of Tudor London.

clue.text: Hymnodist in serene alexandrines?

indicators.note: in shows that the letters sit inside the run of the following words

explanation.surface: A hymn writer composing calm twelve-syllable lines.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run across the join of 'sereNE ALExandrines'.
explanation.definitionFit: John Mason Neale wrote and translated many hymns, including Good King Wenceslas.

clue.text: Composer offers work of fiction to behold

parts.note: a novel is a long work of fiction
lo is an old word meaning look or behold

explanation.surface: A songwriter presents a story for us to admire.
explanation.definitionFit: Ivor Novello was a Welsh songwriter and actor, writer of Keep the Home Fires Burning.

clue.text: Bounder in song by Sidney

indicators.note: in puts the word for a bounder inside the word for a song

parts.note: an aria is a song in an opera
a cad or bounder is a dishonourable man

explanation.surface: A rogue appears in a lyric by the Elizabethan poet Sidney.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Philip Sidney's prose romance The Countess of Pembroke's Arcadia is his best-known work.

clue.text: "When av'rice, luxury and ease / A - - generation please" (Allan Ramsay)

definitions.text: When av'rice, luxury and ease / A - - generation please" (Allan Ramsay)

parts.words: When av'rice, luxury and ease / A - - generation please" (Allan Ramsay)
parts.note: the gap is a compound adjective for people pale from drinking an imported hot brew, Ramsay mocking luxury

explanation.surface: Lines from the Scots poet Allan Ramsay deploring a softened, pampered age.
explanation.walkthrough: A fill-in: Ramsay sneers at a generation with complexions sallow from the new fashion for drinking tea, with the elided Scots spelling.
explanation.definitionFit: Pale-complexioned from the luxury of the tea table, a sign of a pampered generation in Ramsay's eyes.

clue.text: Scott's "wise wight" was black

parts.note: Sir Walter Scott's 1816 novel The Black ... centres on a misshapen recluse thought to be a wise wight

explanation.surface: A note on a magical creature in a Walter Scott tale.
explanation.walkthrough: Scott's The Black Dwarf tells of Elshender, a deformed hermit whom locals take for an uncanny 'wise wight'.
explanation.definitionFit: Scott's novel title names its hero by his very small stature, a person of stunted growth.

clue.text: Inexperienced writers without serious failings?

parts.note: no means without, as in no money
vices are serious moral failings

explanation.surface: New authors are so green they have no bad habits.
explanation.definitionFit: Beginners or learners in a craft are people without experience.

clue.text: Tate's cure-all

definitions.meaning: Nahum Tate, the Poet Laureate, wrote a poem praising tea under this title

explanation.surface: A poet's universal remedy.
explanation.definitionFit: A universal remedy, and the title of Nahum Tate's poem in praise of tea.

clue.text: Possibly con lady (but not Artemis) in ancient city

indicators.note: possibly says the letters of the following words may be arranged another way

explanation.surface: A confidence trickster who may be a woman, not the goddess, in an old city.
explanation.walkthrough: '(but not Artemis)' is surface colour: Artemis sent the boar that ravaged this Greek city, setting up the Calydonian hunt.
explanation.definitionFit: Calydon was a city of ancient Aetolia in Greece, famous for the boar hunt.

clue.text: Parts were named in this city guide

definitions.meaning: Henry Reed's 1946 poetry collection contains Naming of Parts
a street plan of an Italian city, the setting of Romeo and Juliet

explanation.surface: A guidebook in which places are given their names.
explanation.walkthrough: Henry Reed's war poem Naming of Parts appeared in his collection A Map of Verona (1946).
explanation.definitionFit: Both the title of Henry Reed's volume holding Naming of Parts and a street plan of the Italian city.
